endocrine disruptor.text: A substance that interferes with hormone systems, often at concentrations far below those that kill. Effects appear as failed reproduction and altered development rather than as death.
endocrine disruptor.why: One of the few grounds on which European approval is refused on hazard alone, without an exposure argument.

endogenous retrovirus.text: A virus that inserted itself into a host genome long ago and stayed, becoming inherited. Roughly eight per cent of human DNA is of this origin.
endogenous retrovirus.why: One of them supplies the protein that builds the placenta - mammalian pregnancy depends on a domesticated virus.

endophyte.text: A fungus or bacterium living inside a plant's tissues without causing disease, often conferring resistance to pests or stress on its host.
endophyte.why: Greek endon (within) plus phyton (plant). Another partnership invisible to a survey that counts plants.

endosymbiosis.text: One organism living inside another, permanently. Mitochondria and chloroplasts are both captured free-living bacteria, so every plant and animal is a former merger.
endosymbiosis.why: The origin of the eukaryotic cell, and the reason the boundary between organism and community is not sharp.

engraftment.text: Whether transplanted organisms actually establish and persist rather than being displaced. It varies enormously between donors and recipients, which is the practical problem with any transplant.
engraftment.why: The reason donor matching matters, in a gut and in a sediment alike.

epibenthic.text: Living on the surface of the seabed rather than buried in it.

epiphyte.text: A plant or alga growing on another plant, using it as a surface rather than feeding on it.
epiphyte.why: Greek epi- (upon) plus phyton (plant). On eelgrass they shade the leaf they sit on.

EQR.text: Ecological quality ratio: the observed value divided by the value expected in an unimpacted reference state, scaled so that 1 is pristine.
EQR.why: An EU device for making incomparable national measurements comparable. Its denominator is modelled, not measured.

erg.text: A sand sea - the dune-covered kind of desert, as opposed to stony or salt desert.
erg.why: Arabic 'irq, a dune field. What makes it hostile is that the surface moves, not that it is dry.

error threshold.text: The mutation rate above which a lineage can no longer preserve its own information and collapses. RNA viruses sit just below it, which is the fastest possible search that still permits replication.
error threshold.why: Deliberately pushing a virus over it is a real antiviral strategy, called lethal mutagenesis.

essential use.text: A proposed rule that the most harmful substances should be permitted only where they are genuinely necessary and no substitute exists - rather than wherever the exposure looks acceptable.
essential use.why: The concept borrowed from how antibiotics are managed, and the closest existing idea to reserving a chemical rather than banning it.

eukaryote.text: An organism whose cells keep their DNA in a nucleus - animals, plants, fungi, and the enormous majority of microbial diversity that is none of the three.
eukaryote.why: Greek eu (well) plus karyon (kernel). Bacteria and archaea are the ones that do not.

eutrophic.text: Over-fed: a water body receiving more nutrient than it can process.
eutrophic.why: Greek eu- (well) plus trophe (nourishment) - literally well-nourished, which is why the word sounds like praise and means the opposite.

eutrophication.text: Over-feeding of a water body: so much nutrient that production outruns what the system can process.
eutrophication.why: Greek eu- (well) plus trophe (nourishment). Literally well-nourished, which is why the word sounds positive and means the opposite.

euxinic.text: Water that is both oxygen-free and carries free sulphide. The worst case.
euxinic.why: From Pontus Euxinus, the Roman name for the Black Sea, whose deep water has been like this throughout recorded history.

exopolymer.text: Sticky long-chain sugars secreted outside the cell. It binds sediment, forms marine gel, and is what makes water feel slippery.
exopolymer.why: Exo- (outside) plus polymer. Marine biologists count it as TEP.

extremophile.text: An organism thriving in conditions that would kill most life - extremes of heat, salt, acidity, pressure or chemistry. The word records our own expectations rather than anything about the organism.
extremophile.why: To the organism the conditions are not extreme. They are simply where it lives.

faecal microbiota transplant.text: Treating a cleared gut by putting a whole functioning community back, without anyone needing to know which member does the work. Cure rates around ninety per cent.
faecal microbiota transplant.why: The same design as putting healthy sediment into failed sediment - proven in one domain and never tried in the other.

fedtemøg.text: Danish, roughly fat-muck: the greasy, foul organic material that accumulates in the water and along the shore. Not a scientific term, and not measured by anything.
fedtemøg.why: Fedt is fat, møg is muck or dung - a word from people who swim, not from a monitoring programme. The same fedt carries skidefedt, literally shitting-fat, which means excellent. Danish attaches the identical root to the best thing and the worst thing on the same beach.

badevand.text: Danish for bathing water. The one marine variable Denmark measures densely, at many stations, for a long time, because it is a public-health duty rather than an ecological one.
badevand.why: It tests for E. coli and enterococci - faecal indicator bacteria. So the best-replicated marine record in the country counts faeces, and everything about algae, fat or the seabed is inferred from something else.

dynd.text: Danish for mud or ooze - the soft organic-rich seabed that holds fine material and gives it up again when the water moves. GEUS maps it as a substrate class: dynd og sandet dynd, mud and sandy mud.
dynd.why: Related to English dung through the same Germanic root: what settles and rots.

Feltmåling.text: Danish for field measurement - the ODA category holding instrument profiles taken in the water: CTD casts, light attenuation, oxygen.

Ferralsol.text: A deeply weathered tropical soil dominated by iron and aluminium oxides, which lock phosphate up so tightly that fertiliser vanishes from availability within weeks.
Ferralsol.why: Ferrum (iron) plus aluminium: named for what is left after everything else has weathered away.

flagellate.text: A single-celled organism that swims using a whip-like tail. In these waters they are the algae that take over when diatoms cannot grow, and they are poorly eaten.

flocculation.text: Fine particles and dissolved organic matter clumping together and settling out, which happens abruptly where fresh water meets salt.
flocculation.why: Latin floccus, a tuft of wool. What the clumps look like.

folk taxonomy.text: A classification based on how things look and what they do, rather than on how they are related. Plants, animals and fungi is one; it predates evolutionary biology and still organises most monitoring.
folk taxonomy.why: Useful and intuitive, and it systematically hides organisms that fall between its categories.

foraminifera.text: Single-celled organisms that build tiny chambered shells. Abundant in sediment, and their shells preserve, which makes them a record of past conditions.
foraminifera.why: Latin foramen (hole) plus ferre (to bear) - the shells are perforated.

founder effect.text: The outsized influence of whoever establishes a population first. Their descendants make up everything that follows, so what they happened to be matters more than what would have suited the place.
founder effect.why: After a crash the survivors are not a random sample - they are whoever tolerated the thing that did the killing, and then they have the place to themselves.

frustule.text: The two-part silica shell of a diatom.

fungi.text: A kingdom of life separate from plants and animals, feeding by absorbing what they have digested outside themselves. On land they are the principal decomposers of tough material; in the sea they are barely studied.
fungi.why: Latin fungus, mushroom - though most fungi never make anything you would recognise as one.

fungicide.text: A chemical designed to kill fungi. Applied in agriculture by the thousand tonnes, and acting on enzyme systems that fungi share with most other life.
fungicide.why: The -cide ending is Latin caedere, to kill - as in pesticide, biocide, herbicide.

gene duplication.text: A copy of a gene arising, leaving one to keep doing the original job while the other is free to change. The main route by which genuinely new functions appear.
gene duplication.why: It is why what already exists constrains what can evolve next.

generation time.text: How long between one generation and the next. It sets the ceiling on how fast a population can adapt, and it differs between a marine bacterium and an eelgrass meadow by roughly five orders of magnitude.
generation time.why: The single most important number in deciding who wins under a novel pressure.

glyphosate.text: The world's most used herbicide. Its target enzyme is absent in animals but present in plants, bacteria and fungi, which makes it an antimicrobial as well as a weedkiller.
glyphosate.why: From glycine and phosphonate, its chemical parts.

grab.text: A sampling device dropped to the seabed that bites out a fixed area of sediment and brings it up. One grab is one sample, and it is how nearly all seabed fauna data is collected.
grab.why: It grabs. The fixed area is what makes counts comparable.

grandfathered.text: Permitted to continue under old rules because it was already in use when new rules arrived. Most industrial chemicals in Europe entered the system this way.
grandfathered.why: From American voting law of the 1890s, where a grandfather clause exempted people whose grandfathers had voted - the origin is not a happy one.

Great Oxidation Event.text: The point around 2.4 billion years ago when oxygen produced by cyanobacteria accumulated in the atmosphere, poisoning most of the biosphere that had produced it and making all later aerobic life possible.
Great Oxidation Event.why: The largest mass extinction there has ever been, caused by a waste product. It is also the clearest case of adapted survivors remaking the conditions for everything after them.

griseofulvin.text: An antifungal drug made by a Penicillium mould to kill other fungi.
griseofulvin.why: One fungus's weapon against its relatives, borrowed for human medicine.

hazard.text: The intrinsic capacity of something to cause harm, independent of whether anyone is exposed to it. A shark in an aquarium is a hazard; a shark in your bath is a risk.
hazard.why: Kept strictly separate from risk in regulatory language, and routinely conflated everywhere else.

Hedley fractionation.text: A sequence of chemical extractions that separates soil phosphorus into pools by how easily it can be released - from immediately available to permanently locked away.
Hedley fractionation.why: The standard soil-science method, and the reason soil scientists never quote total phosphorus alone.

helminth.text: A parasitic worm. Their removal from human populations is implicated in immune dysregulation, which is the standard cautionary case for eliminating an organism whose full role was unknown.

heterotroph.text: An organism that gets its carbon by consuming organic matter made by something else. All animals and fungi, and most bacteria.

holobiont.text: An organism considered together with all the microbes living in and on it, as one functioning unit - because for many purposes that is what it actually is.
holobiont.why: Greek holos (whole) plus bios. A word that exists because the older picture of an organism turned out to be incomplete.

horizontal gene transfer.text: Genes moving sideways between unrelated organisms rather than down from parent to offspring. Bacteria do it routinely, which is why a resistance evolved once can appear everywhere.
horizontal gene transfer.why: The reason prokaryotic adaptation is not limited by the lineage that happened to invent it. Eukaryotes have almost no equivalent.

humus.text: The dark, stable remains of decayed organic matter in soil, after everything easily eaten has gone.
humus.why: Latin humus, ground or earth - the same root as human and humble.

hydrogeology.text: The study of how water moves through rock and soil underground. Nitrogen retention is a hydrogeological quantity as much as a biological one.

hydrophobic.text: Water-repelling. Such substances leave the water and gather at surfaces - which is why they concentrate in the microlayer and in fatty tissue.

hydrothermal vent.text: A seafloor hot spring where water heated by rock emerges carrying hydrogen sulphide and metals. The communities around them run entirely on chemical energy, with no sunlight anywhere in the food chain.
hydrothermal vent.why: Discovered in 1977, which overturned the assumption that all life ultimately depends on the sun.

hypovirulence.text: A pathogen made less harmful, usually by its own infection with something else. The basis of using a virus to control a fungal disease of plants.
hypovirulence.why: Not killing the pathogen but taking its weapons away.

hypoxia.text: Not enough oxygen. Conventionally below 4 mg per litre in marine work, with 2 mg/l as severe.
hypoxia.why: Greek hypo- (under) plus oxys, the root in oxygen.

hysteresis.text: A system that does not retrace its path: the conditions that would restore it are not the conditions that broke it. Easy to enter, hard to leave.
hysteresis.why: Greek hysteresis, a shortcoming or lagging behind.

idempotent.text: Doing it again changes nothing. A niche is either occupied or it is not, so there is no dose to escalate and no gradient for anything to adapt along.
idempotent.why: Borrowed from mathematics and computing, and unusually apt: it names exactly what distinguishes exclusion from a chemical weapon.

iltsvind.text: Danish for oxygen depletion - literally oxygen-dwindling. The word used in Danish public debate for what happens when the seabed suffocates.
iltsvind.why: Ilt is Danish for oxygen, coined by H.C. Orsted from ild, fire.

immobilisation.text: The opposite of mineralisation: microbes taking dissolved nutrient out of the water or soil to build their own bodies. High-carbon, low-nitrogen material causes it.
immobilisation.why: The nutrient is not destroyed, just made unavailable while it sits inside a bacterium.

in situ.text: In place - an experiment or measurement made where the thing actually lives, rather than in a laboratory.

indsatsbehov.text: Danish for the required effort - the calculated size of the reduction a water body needs to reach its target. The central number of the whole nitrogen policy.

infauna.text: Animals living inside the sediment rather than on top of it - worms, clams, the things a grab sample catches.
infauna.why: Latin in- plus fauna. The ones you have to dig for.

innate immunity.text: The defence system built in advance to recognise general signatures of infection, as against the adaptive system that learns individual ones. Plants and invertebrates have only this - and much of it turns out to be homologous to bacterial anti-phage machinery.
innate immunity.why: Which makes part of our own immune system a captured weapon from the microbial war.

inoculum.text: A small quantity of living material introduced deliberately to establish a community - a spoonful of healthy sediment, a starter culture.
inoculum.why: Latin inoculare, to graft in. The plural is inocula.

invertebrate.text: An animal without a backbone - worms, molluscs, crustaceans, insects. The overwhelming majority of animal species, and nearly everything on a seabed.
invertebrate.why: Latin in- (not) plus vertebra. Defined by what it lacks, which tells you who wrote the category.

IoT.text: Internet of things - cheap networked devices that report readings without anyone visiting them. In an environmental context the appeal is replication rather than precision.
IoT.why: For testing whether one station can represent an area, forty rough sensors beat one perfect one, because the question is about variance.

isotherm.text: A curve showing how much of a substance a material will hold at each concentration, measured at one temperature. The standard way to describe a soil's capacity to hold phosphate.
isotherm.why: Greek isos (equal) plus therme (heat) - the temperature is held constant.

Kd.text: The light attenuation coefficient: how fast light dies away with depth. Higher Kd means darker at the bottom.
Kd.why: One broadband number standing in for a whole spectrum, which is why its cause cannot be read off it.

kill the winner.text: The model in which whichever organism is most abundant is the easiest target for its own specific virus, so cropping falls hardest on the winner and diversity is maintained by predation rather than by competition.
kill the winner.why: It makes viruses a structuring force rather than only a destructive one.

klapplads.text: Danish for a licensed site where dredged material is dumped at sea. There are 114 of them.
klapplads.why: Klappe, to tip or dump; plads, place.

Krebs cycle.text: The central loop of metabolism, by which cells extract energy from food. Present in essentially all aerobic life.
Krebs cycle.why: Hans Krebs, 1937. Also called the citric acid cycle, after the first compound in it.

labile.text: Easily and quickly broken down. Sugars and fresh algal material are labile.
labile.why: Latin labilis, liable to slip or fall. Its opposite here is recalcitrant.

Labyrinthula.text: The slime-mould-like organism that causes eelgrass wasting disease. It destroyed most Atlantic eelgrass in the 1930s and is still present.
Labyrinthula.why: Named for the labyrinth of tracks its cells glide along.

labyrinthulid.text: A group of marine organisms that glide along self-made slime tracks and decompose organic matter - and include the one that causes eelgrass wasting disease. Neither fungi nor animals nor plants.
labyrinthulid.why: Named for the labyrinth of tracks their cells move along. Barely studied, and almost certainly under-appreciated.

Leptosol.text: A very shallow soil, under about 25 cm to rock. Almost no capacity to buffer anything.

lethal mutagenesis.text: Pushing a virus above its error threshold on purpose, so that it mutates itself out of existence. It works because the strategy that makes RNA viruses fast is also the thing that can be turned against them.
lethal mutagenesis.why: One of the few antiviral approaches that a pathogen cannot straightforwardly evolve around.

Liebig.text: The law of the minimum: growth is set by whichever necessary thing is scarcest, not by the total of everything supplied. Ten nutrients in surplus and one missing gives you no growth.
Liebig.why: Justus von Liebig, the 19th-century chemist who argued it for crops. The name carries none of the meaning, which is why it is worth spelling out.

lignin.text: The rigid material that makes wood woody. It is the hardest common biological molecule to break down, and mainly fungi do it.
lignin.why: Latin lignum, wood. Nitrogen enrichment suppresses the enzymes that degrade it, which is why it accumulates.

local adaptation.text: A population fitted to the specific conditions it has lived in, often over very many generations. It is why a transplanted community is at a disadvantage against residents on their own ground.
local adaptation.why: And why a donor community has to come from a matched setting, or the survivors it must displace simply win.

lucinid.text: A family of clams that host sulphide-oxidising bacteria in their gills. In seagrass beds they keep the root zone habitable.
lucinid.why: The three-way partnership of plant, clam and bacterium was only described in 2012.

Lysprocent.text: Danish for light percentage - the share of surface light still present at a given depth, already computed in the ODA record. Eelgrass needs roughly 11 to 14 percent.
Lysprocent.why: Lys (light) plus procent. It is the number the eelgrass requirement is written in.

macroalgae.text: Seaweed - algae large enough to see, attached to rock or shell rather than drifting.
macroalgae.why: Macro, large, as against the microscopic plankton.

macrofauna.text: The animals big enough to be caught on a one-millimetre sieve - worms, clams, crustaceans. What a seabed sample is counted as.
macrofauna.why: Macro, large. Below them are meiofauna, below those, microbes.

MARPOL.text: The international convention governing pollution from ships. It sets what a vessel may legally discharge at sea - sewage, greywater, food waste, scrubber washwater - and where.
MARPOL.why: MARine POLlution, contracted. Compliance is the baseline, not the absence of discharge.

meiofauna.text: The very small animals between sand grains - nematodes and tiny crustaceans. Too big to be microbes, too small for the sieves used on macrofauna.

mesocosm.text: An experimental container big enough to hold a working piece of an ecosystem, but small enough to control - a tank, an enclosure, a bag in the sea.
mesocosm.why: Greek mesos (middle) plus kosmos (world): between a test tube and the real thing.

mesozooplankton.text: The middle size class of drifting animals, chiefly copepods - between a fifth of a millimetre and two centimetres. The link between algae and fish.

metabarcoding.text: Sequencing DNA from a bulk sample to list what organisms are present, without anyone having to identify them by eye. Taxonomically agnostic by construction, which is exactly why it finds things the categories missed.
metabarcoding.why: Barcoding is identifying one specimen by a short DNA sequence; meta- is doing it to a whole community at once.

microbiome.text: The community of microbes living in and on an organism, which for many purposes is part of that organism - performing digestion, defence and nutrition it cannot perform alone.
microbiome.why: Micro plus biome. A word that exists because the older picture of an individual organism turned out to be incomplete.

microlayer.text: The top few micrometres of the sea, which concentrate surfactants, fats and hydrophobic pollutants far above their concentration in the bulk water.
microlayer.why: It is the layer a swimmer's skin actually passes through.

micronutrient.text: An element needed in tiny amounts but needed absolutely - iron, zinc, copper, cobalt, molybdenum, selenium. Absence is as fatal as absence of nitrogen.
micronutrient.why: As against macronutrients: carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and the rest needed in bulk.

microphytobenthos.text: Microscopic algae living on the sediment surface. Their secreted polymer glues the grains together and raises the current needed to erode the bed.
microphytobenthos.why: Micro (small) plus phyton (plant) plus benthos (the depths): the tiny plants of the bottom.

mineralisation.text: The breakdown of organic material back into simple inorganic compounds - releasing the nutrients that were locked in tissue.
mineralisation.why: Turning organic matter back into minerals. Remineralisation is the same word for material that was mineral to start with.

mitochondria.text: The compartments in which eukaryotic cells carry out respiration. Descended from captured bacteria, and present in fungi, plants and animals alike - which is why respiratory poisons are rarely selective.
mitochondria.why: Greek mitos (thread) plus chondros (grain), from how they look under a microscope.

mor.text: Raw, matted, unincorporated humus sitting on top of the soil because the fauna that would mix it in are absent or excluded.
mor.why: Also from Danish, meaning mould in the other sense. The terrestrial version of an organic mat on the seabed.

mucus layer.text: The gel coating animal surfaces exposed to the outside. It is enriched in bacteriophage, which attack incoming bacteria - a defence delivered by something classified as a parasite.
mucus layer.why: Which is the pathogen-and-partner distinction failing again, in the place a body meets the world.

mull.text: Humus that soil animals have worked into the mineral soil - crumbly, fast-cycling, well mixed.
mull.why: From Danish and German muld, mould or loose earth. Its degraded counterpart is mor.

mutation rate.text: How often the genetic code changes when it is copied. Combined with population size it sets how much variation a lineage generates per unit time, and therefore how quickly it can meet something new.
mutation rate.why: A large population with a short generation explores more possibilities in a year than a small slow one does in a century.

mutational bias.text: The fact that mutation is not uniform across a genome. Rates vary with chromatin state, transcription and sequence context; stress induces mutagenesis; recombination concentrates at hotspots.
mutational bias.why: Variation is structured, and the structure is itself an evolved product of what the lineage has met before - which is priming, one level down.

mutualism.text: A relationship in which both partners benefit. The word English lacks is a common antonym for pathogen - we named the harmful relationships and left the rest to be called symbionts, which technically covers all of them.
mutualism.why: The vocabulary itself is biased toward harm, which is worth noticing when reading any list of species.

mycobiome.text: The fungal community of a place or a host, as distinct from its bacteria. Marine sediments are turning out to hold far more fungal diversity than anyone expected.
mycobiome.why: Myco (fungus) on the pattern of microbiome. The word is recent because the recognition is recent.

mycoparasitism.text: A fungus parasitising another fungus. It is how Trichoderma protects crops, and it is the fungal diagonal of the same matrix.
mycoparasitism.why: Fungi against fungi, sold in a bag.

mycorrhiza.text: The partnership between plant roots and fungi that feeds the plant phosphorus in exchange for carbon. Heavy fertilising suppresses it.

mycovirus.text: A virus that infects fungi. Some weaken their host rather than killing it, and one that weakens chestnut blight is a deployed biocontrol agent - a virus protecting a tree by disarming a fungus.
mycovirus.why: Antifungals of viral variety, and a working demonstration that the whole matrix is real.

målbelastning.text: Danish for target load - how much nitrogen a water body may receive and still meet its environmental objective.

natural experiment.text: A change imposed by circumstance rather than by a researcher, which happens to create a comparison. Dated construction works, staggered policy adoption and closures all qualify.
natural experiment.why: The nearest thing to an experiment available when the system is too large to manipulate on purpose.

necromass.text: Dead biomass. In soil, dead microbes themselves make up a large share of the lasting organic matter.

nematode.text: A roundworm. In sediment they are microscopic, enormously abundant, and among the last animals left when conditions get bad.

neonicotinoid.text: The most widely used insecticide class. It acts on acetylcholine receptors, which every animal with a nervous system has, including all marine invertebrates.
neonicotinoid.why: Nicotine-like, and acting at the same receptor nicotine does.

nitrate.text: The oxidised, stable form of dissolved nitrogen, and the form that leaches from farmland into groundwater and streams.

nitrification.text: Bacteria oxidising ammonium to nitrate. It consumes oxygen - 4.57 grams per gram of nitrogen - without anything growing.
nitrification.why: From nitre, saltpetre, the old name for nitrate salts.

nitrogenase.text: The enzyme that lets some bacteria pull nitrogen straight out of the air. It requires molybdenum or vanadium, and it is destroyed by oxygen.
nitrogenase.why: The -ase ending marks an enzyme throughout biochemistry.

NOVANA.text: Denmark's national programme for monitoring water and nature. Almost every Danish environmental number ultimately comes from it.
NOVANA.why: Danish acronym: the national programme for monitoring of the aquatic environment and nature.

occlusion.text: Sorbed material becoming physically enclosed inside a mineral, so it can no longer be released at all. The one-way end of sorption.
occlusion.why: Latin occludere, to shut up or close off.

oligotrophic.text: Nutrient-poor, low production, usually clear water.
oligotrophic.why: Greek oligos, few. The other end of the same scale as eutrophic.

oomycete.text: A fungus-like group including Pythium and Phytophthora - water moulds that swim as spores and attack stressed roots. They are not actually fungi despite living like them.

opisthokont.text: The branch containing animals and fungi together. They are sister lineages: a mushroom is a closer relative of yours than of a plant.
opisthokont.why: Greek opisthen (behind) plus kontos (pole), after the single rear-facing tail on a sperm cell and a fungal spore alike.

optode.text: An oxygen sensor that measures how a dye's glow is quenched by oxygen. It replaced chemical titration, and the two do not always agree.

overløb.text: Danish for a sewer overflow - untreated sewage discharged directly when rain overwhelms a combined system.
overløb.why: Over plus løb (run). Denmark has 19,665 registered outfall points.

parasitism.text: A relationship in which one partner benefits at the other's expense. The same organism can be a parasite in one host or one condition and harmless in another.
parasitism.why: Greek parasitos, one who eats beside another - originally a hanger-on at somebody else's dinner.

pathobiont.text: A resident organism that is harmless most of the time and becomes harmful when conditions change - the host is stressed, the community shifts, a barrier fails.
pathobiont.why: The word exists because the pathogen and non-pathogen categories could not hold.

PBT.text: Persistent, Bioaccumulative and Toxic - the three-part test that gets a substance refused outright in some European approvals, with no exposure argument allowed to rescue it.
PBT.why: vPvB is the stronger version: very Persistent and very Bioaccumulative, where persistence alone carries the case.

PE.text: Population equivalent - the standard unit of sewage load, one person's daily contribution. Industrial discharges are expressed in how many people they equal.
PE.why: Lets a dairy and a town be added together.

pelagic.text: Of the open water column, as opposed to the bed.
pelagic.why: Greek pelagos, the open sea. Its counterpart is benthic.

peroxidase.text: An enzyme that neutralises reactive oxygen inside a cell. The selenium-dependent version is why selenium is essential.
peroxidase.why: It disposes of peroxides, which would otherwise do damage.

phage therapy.text: Treating a bacterial infection with the viruses that attack that bacterium. Used clinically in Georgia and Poland for decades and being revived against resistant infections.
phage therapy.why: Antibacterials of viral variety - the matrix of microbial warfare filled in from a direction Western medicine largely skipped.

pharmacokinetic.text: To do with how much of a substance an organism takes up, where it goes, and how fast it is broken down - as opposed to what it does once it arrives.
pharmacokinetic.why: Greek pharmakon (drug) plus kinesis (movement). Selectivity that is pharmacokinetic is selectivity of exposure, not of mechanism.

phenology.text: The timing of biological events through the year - when things spawn, bloom, migrate - and whether two events that need to coincide still do.
phenology.why: Greek phainein, to appear. The study of when things show up.

phosphate.text: The dissolved form of phosphorus. It binds tightly to iron oxides in oxygenated sediment and is released again when the sediment loses its oxygen.
phosphate.why: That release is the single strongest feedback loop in a eutrophic system.

photoinhibition.text: Too much light damaging the photosynthetic machinery. The ceiling of the light window.
photoinhibition.why: Light doing the inhibiting - the reason clearest is not always best.

photosynthesis.text: Building organic matter from carbon dioxide using light, releasing oxygen. Respiration is the same reaction run backwards, which is why the two gases move in opposite directions.

photosystem II.text: The protein complex that splits water and starts photosynthesis. Triazine and urea herbicides block it, which makes them equally effective against algae.
photosystem II.why: The second of two photosystems, named in the order they were discovered rather than the order they act.

Phytophthora.text: A genus of water mould that destroys plant roots. The potato blight that caused the Irish famine was one of these.

phytoplankton.text: The drifting microscopic plants of the water column - diatoms, flagellates, cyanobacteria. Everything else in the sea ultimately eats them or eats something that did.

phytotoxin.text: A substance that poisons plants. Waterlogged ground makes several of its own - organic acids, ethylene, sulphide, and reduced iron and manganese.

picomolar.text: A concentration of one trillionth of a mole per litre. Vitamins and some trace metals matter to marine life at concentrations this small.
picomolar.why: The prefix pico means a trillionth.

picoplankton.text: The smallest plankton, under two thousandths of a millimetre. Too small for most grazers to catch, so what eats them is mostly viruses.
picoplankton.why: Pico, a trillionth - here just meaning very small indeed.

plankton.text: Anything living in the water column that drifts rather than swims against the current, from bacteria to jellyfish.
plankton.why: Greek planktos, wandering. It describes a way of life, not a group of relatives.

polychaete.text: A marine bristle worm. Many build tubes that stabilise sediment; others burrow and mix it. A large share of what a seabed sample contains.

polymerase.text: The enzyme that copies genetic material. How accurately it does so sets a lineage's mutation rate, and therefore which of the two adaptive strategies is available to it.
polymerase.why: From polymer plus -ase, the enzyme ending.

porewater.text: The water in the spaces between sediment grains. Its chemistry is often wholly different from the water above, and it is what a buried animal actually lives in.

precautionary principle.text: The idea that action to prevent harm need not wait for full scientific certainty. Written into EU law, and constrained in practice by requirements of proportionality.
precautionary principle.why: Article 191 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. Invoked more often than it decides anything.

priming.text: Having machinery already close to what a new situation requires. New biological capabilities almost never arise from nothing - they arise by duplicating and modifying something that already worked - so the distance from existing machinery to the needed function matters more than the supply of mutations.
priming.why: Antibiotic resistance appeared in years because soil bacteria had competed with antibiotic-making fungi for hundreds of millions of years, so efflux pumps and degrading enzymes were already in the shared gene pool. Nylon-oligomer digestion appeared within decades of nylon existing, on an entirely synthetic substrate, because amide hydrolysis is ordinary chemistry that everything already does.

priority effect.text: Arriving first being worth more than being well suited. It means the composition of a recovered community records its history as much as its conditions.
priority effect.why: The reason a degraded state can persist after the conditions that caused it have gone, with no other mechanism required.

probiotic.text: A live organism given deliberately to establish or restore a community. Used in aquaculture in place of antibiotics for the same reason it works in a gut.
probiotic.why: Literally for-life, coined against antibiotic, against-life.

prokaryote.text: An organism whose cell has no nucleus - bacteria and archaea. They run essentially every chemical transformation in the sea that is not photosynthesis or animal respiration.
prokaryote.why: Greek pro (before) plus karyon (kernel): named for lacking the thing eukaryotes have, which tells you who was doing the naming.

proofreading.text: The error-correcting step a polymerase performs while copying genetic material. RNA viruses mostly lack it, which is why they mutate orders of magnitude faster than anything cellular.
proofreading.why: The absence is not a defect. It is what makes their strategy possible.

propagule.text: Whatever a species uses to start a new individual somewhere else - a larva, a seed, a spore, a fragment.
propagule.why: Latin propagare, to propagate. The unit of arrival.

protist.text: A catch-all for single-celled organisms with a nucleus that are not animals, plants or fungi. Includes most marine algae and many parasites.

pycnocline.text: The depth at which density changes sharply, separating lighter water above from denser water below. It acts as a lid: below it, oxygen is not replaced.

pyrethroid.text: A synthetic insecticide acting on voltage-gated sodium channels - universal in animals. Crustaceans are extremely sensitive, being arthropods like the intended targets.
pyrethroid.why: Modelled on pyrethrins from chrysanthemum flowers.

Pythium.text: A water mould that rots seedlings and roots, thriving where soil or sediment is waterlogged and low in oxygen.
Pythium.why: The classic damping-off disease of a wet greenhouse.

Q10.text: How much faster a biological process runs for every ten degrees of warming. Around two for most decay, meaning respiration roughly doubles.
Q10.why: A rule of thumb old enough to have no better name.

quasispecies.text: A population that exists as a cloud of related variants rather than as a defined genotype, because it mutates faster than selection can purify it. Selection then acts on the cloud rather than on any individual sequence.
quasispecies.why: The normal condition for RNA viruses, and the reason a virus is better thought of as a distribution than as a thing.

r-selected.text: Organisms that bet on speed and numbers - short lives, fast growth, many offspring, few requirements. They dominate disturbed and unstable conditions.
r-selected.why: From r, the growth-rate term in the population equation. Its counterpart is K-selected: slow, large, long-lived, competitive in stable conditions.

radial oxygen loss.text: Rooted plants leaking oxygen from their roots into the sediment, which keeps sulphide away from the root. It is powered by photosynthesis, so shade shuts it off.
radial oxygen loss.why: Radial because it moves outward from the root, not along it.

REACH.text: The EU regulation governing industrial chemicals. Its slogan is 'no data, no market' - the duty to supply safety data sits with whoever wants to sell the substance.
REACH.why: Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation and restriction of CHemicals. The data required scales with tonnage, so small-volume substances are barely characterised.

recalcitrant.text: Resistant to decay. Lignin, humic material, and most synthetic compounds.
recalcitrant.why: Latin recalcitrare, to kick back - literally to dig the heels in.

recombination.text: The shuffling of genetic material during sexual reproduction. It concentrates at particular locations rather than falling evenly, and mate choice ahead of it is under selection - so none of it is a lottery.
recombination.why: The popular picture of random variation is wrong at every stage of this.

Redfield.text: The roughly fixed ratio of carbon to nitrogen to phosphorus in marine plankton, about 106:16:1 by atoms. It lets you convert one nutrient into an expected amount of biomass, or of oxygen demand.
Redfield.why: Alfred Redfield noticed in 1934 that plankton and seawater share the ratio, which is either a coincidence or the plankton setting the chemistry of the ocean.

redox.text: Whether the chemistry of a place is oxidising or reducing - broadly, whether oxygen is available. It governs which reactions run and which metals stay put.

reductase.text: An enzyme that reduces a compound - adds electrons to it. Nitrate reductase is the one that lets an organism use nitrate.
reductase.why: Also an enzyme, named for what it does.

remineralisation.text: Decay: organic matter broken back down to its dissolved inorganic constituents, releasing the nutrients and consuming oxygen.
remineralisation.why: Turning organic material back into minerals.

replication.text: Taking more than one measurement of the same thing, so that variability can be told apart from difference. Without it, one sample is indistinguishable from a whole area.
replication.why: The single most common thing missing from environmental monitoring designs.

residual estimator.text: A quantity computed as whatever is left after subtracting everything you did model from a measured total. It is never itself measured, and it absorbs every error in every other term.
residual estimator.why: Which is why such a figure can come out negative, and why a negative one is the method reporting its own error bars.

resistance.text: The evolved ability to survive a dose that would once have been lethal. Its appearance is simultaneously evidence that the organism was exposed and that the exposure was selecting.
resistance.why: The same phenomenon in bacteria facing antibiotics, fungi facing fungicides, and weeds facing herbicides - and for the same reason.

respiration.text: Extracting energy from organic matter, consuming oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide. The reverse of photosynthesis, and what decay is at the chemical level.
respiration.why: The reason every corpse relieves a carbon shortage and deepens an oxygen one.

restriction enzyme.text: A bacterial protein that cuts foreign DNA at a specific sequence, defending against phage. Its discovery made molecular biology possible.
restriction enzyme.why: The other great tool taken off the same battlefield.

resuspension.text: Sediment lifted back into the water by waves, currents or gear, after having settled.
resuspension.why: It returns buried material, and its chemistry, to circulation.

retention.text: The share of nitrogen applied on land that never reaches the sea, because it is taken up, denitrified or stored on the way. The largest single number in the whole account, and one its own producers say cannot be measured directly.
retention.why: Latin retinere, to hold back. It is a modelled quantity presented as a map.

return interval.text: How long between one disturbance and the next. Compared against how long recovery takes, it decides whether a system persists in an early state permanently or reaches maturity between hits.
return interval.why: The number that matters for trawling, and the one an annual effort figure cannot express.

rhizosphere.text: The thin zone of soil or sediment immediately around a root, chemically and biologically quite unlike the bulk material a few millimetres away.
rhizosphere.why: Greek rhiza (root) plus sphaira. Where the plant and the microbial world actually meet.

råstof.text: Danish for raw material - here, licensed extraction of sand and gravel from the seabed. 305 areas are designated.

salinity.text: How much salt is dissolved in water. Open ocean is about 35 grams per kilogram; the Baltic is a fraction of that.
salinity.why: The gradient through Danish waters is one of the sharpest anywhere.

salting-out.text: Substances becoming less soluble as salinity rises, so they come out of solution into films, droplets and aggregates.
salting-out.why: Adding salt pushes things out of the water. It is why fats behave differently in the sea than in a lake.

saprotroph.text: An organism that feeds on dead material, breaking it down. Most fungi are saprotrophs, and they handle the tough fractions bacteria leave behind.

SDHI.text: A fungicide class blocking succinate dehydrogenase, which is simultaneously complex II of the respiratory chain and a step in the Krebs cycle. Conserved wherever there are mitochondria.
SDHI.why: Succinate dehydrogenase inhibitor. The target does two jobs, so blocking it stops two processes.

seagrass.text: A true flowering plant that lives submerged in the sea, rooted in sediment - not a seaweed. Eelgrass is Denmark's species.
seagrass.why: Grass-like in appearance only; it is more closely related to lilies than to grass.

Secchi.text: The oldest instrument in oceanography: a white disc lowered until it disappears. The depth at which it vanishes is a measure of water clarity, and the record goes back over a century.
Secchi.why: Angelo Secchi, papal astronomer, 1865. Still in use because it is simple and comparable.

sediment sickness.text: Ground in which a plant will not grow although the chemistry looks adequate, because of accumulated pathogens, lost symbionts, or autotoxic residues.
sediment sickness.why: Horticulture calls the same thing replant disease and tests it by swapping the soil.

sedimentation.text: Particles settling out of the water onto the bed.
sedimentation.why: The opposite process to resuspension, and the two together decide what the bed is made of.

Sedimentkemi.text: Danish for sediment chemistry - the ODA category holding what has been measured in the bed itself, as opposed to the water above it.
Sedimentkemi.why: The category this project repeatedly finds nearly empty of the analytes that matter.

selection pressure.text: Any condition that kills or hinders some individuals more than others, so that the survivors' traits become more common. Applying a biocide is applying one deliberately.
selection pressure.why: A dose too low to kill outright is not neutral - it is the regime in which selection is strongest, because it kills enough to matter and spares enough to breed.

self-amplifying.text: A feedback where the effect makes its own cause stronger. Oxygen depletion is one: the casualties decay, the decay consumes more oxygen.
self-amplifying.why: Also called positive feedback, which is misleading because nothing about it is good.

self-correcting.text: A feedback where the effect undoes its own cause. Carbon dioxide depletion is one: whatever dies of it decays and puts the carbon back.
self-correcting.why: Also called negative feedback. The two words are about direction, not about desirability.

Shelford.text: The law of tolerance: every requirement has a ceiling as well as a floor. Too much of a needed thing kills as surely as too little.
Shelford.why: Victor Shelford, an American ecologist, 1913. Liebig gives you the floor; Shelford gives you the roof.

shikimate.text: A biochemical pathway that makes aromatic amino acids. Plants, bacteria and fungi have it; animals do not, and must eat those amino acids instead.
shikimate.why: Named after shikimi, the Japanese star anise from which the acid was first isolated.

silicate.text: Dissolved silicon. Diatoms need it to build their shells, and it comes only from rock weathering, so human activity raises nitrogen and phosphorus but never this.
silicate.why: The changing ratio is why diatoms give way to flagellates.

sill.text: An underwater ridge across the mouth of a basin. Water below the sill depth cannot flow out or be replaced from the side, so it stagnates.
sill.why: The same word as a door sill - a threshold you have to get over.

sonde.text: An instrument lowered into water to record conditions as it descends. The record names which sonde was used, which is what makes instrument changes testable.
sonde.why: French sonde, a sounding line - the rope with a weight that measured depth before electronics.

sorption.text: A substance sticking to a solid surface, covering both adsorption onto it and absorption into it. Phosphate sorbs to iron oxides, which is how soil holds it.
sorption.why: The umbrella term when you do not want to commit to which of the two is happening.

speciation.text: In chemistry, which chemical form an element is in - dissolved, bound to a particle, complexed with an organic molecule. Toxicity and availability both depend on it, and a total measurement hides it.
speciation.why: Nothing to do with the biological sense of new species arising.

stepped wedge.text: A trial design in which every participant eventually receives the treatment, but the order is randomised. Each is its own control before crossover, and a control for the others after.
stepped wedge.why: It makes a randomised comparison possible where withholding the treatment from anyone would be politically or ethically impossible.

sterol.text: A class of molecules that stiffen cell membranes - cholesterol in animals, ergosterol in fungi, phytosterols in plants. Every eukaryote makes one, by broadly the same route.
sterol.why: Which is why azole fungicides, which block that route, cannot be selective for fungi in principle.

stoichiometry.text: The fixed proportions in which substances combine, and so how much of one thing a given amount of another can produce or consume.

stramenopile.text: A major branch of the eukaryotic tree containing diatoms, brown algae and kelp, oomycetes and labyrinthulids. Its members look like plants, fungi and moulds respectively, and are none of those things.
stramenopile.why: Latin stramen (straw) plus pilus (hair), after the fine hairs on one of their two swimming tails. Also called heterokonts, for the same reason.

stratification.text: Water settled into layers that do not mix, because the upper water is warmer or fresher and therefore lighter.
stratification.why: Latin stratum, a layer. It is what makes deep water run out of oxygen.

stressor.text: Anything that pushes an organism or system away from the conditions it functions in. The ecological term of art for a cause of harm.
stressor.why: Borrowed from physiology, where it means the same and was equally vague.

strobilurin.text: A major fungicide class that blocks complex III of the mitochondrial respiratory chain - the machinery by which anything with mitochondria breathes.
strobilurin.why: Derived from a compound made by the fungus Strobilurus, which uses it against its competitors.

sublethal.text: An effect that does not kill: impaired growth, reproduction, behaviour or immunity. Standard toxicity testing measures death, so sublethal harm is systematically under-recorded.
sublethal.why: Below the lethal dose. The organism is counted as a survivor.

sulphate.text: The dissolved sulphur compound that makes up a large part of sea salt. Harmless in itself, and the raw material bacteria turn into sulphide once oxygen is gone.
sulphate.why: Seawater holds about 2.7 grams per litre; fresh water holds a hundredth of that.

sulphide.text: The chemical made when bacteria breathe sulphate instead of oxygen. It smells of rotten eggs, is toxic to almost everything, and consumes oxygen the moment it meets any.
sulphide.why: Seawater carries so much sulphate that once oxygen runs out, sulphide production is effectively unlimited.

sulphidic.text: Containing free sulphide. A sulphidic sediment is one where sulphate reduction has taken over and the bed has turned toxic.
sulphidic.why: The condition that follows anoxia in salt water, and does not follow it in fresh.

superinfection exclusion.text: A cell already infected by one virus resisting infection by another. The resident virus defends its host, in its own interest.
superinfection exclusion.why: Virus against virus - and the basis of deliberately infecting a crop with a mild strain to keep a severe one out.

suppressive.text: A soil whose microbial community actively prevents disease. The property is transferable: mix a little into a diseased soil and it becomes suppressive too.
suppressive.why: Suppressive of the pathogen, not of the plant.

surfactant.text: A substance that lowers surface tension and gathers at the air-water boundary. Detergents, and many natural molecules.

Svanemærket.text: The Nordic Swan ecolabel. A lifecycle standard with criteria set by a Nordic board, verified by third parties, tightened periodically, and awarded only to the better performers in a category.
Svanemærket.why: It restricts substances that are entirely legal, which is what makes its existence evidence about where the legal floor sits.

swept-area.text: How much of the seabed fishing gear has dragged across, expressed as a ratio: 2 means the area was covered twice over in a year.
swept-area.why: The standard measure of trawling pressure. Published annually, which cannot show how often a given patch is hit.

symbiont.text: One partner in a symbiosis. Often the smaller and less visible one, and often the one a survey does not count.
symbiont.why: From symbiosis: Greek syn (together) plus bios (life).

symbiosis.text: Two species living in close, lasting partnership. It ranges from both benefiting to one exploiting the other, and much of it was invisible to science until molecular methods arrived.

syncytin.text: The protein that fuses cells into the layer through which a mammalian placenta exchanges nutrients. It is a viral envelope gene, captured and kept.
syncytin.why: The single clearest case of a pathogen becoming essential.

take-all decline.text: A wheat disease that subsides on its own if the same field is cropped long enough, because Pseudomonas populations build up in the soil until they suppress it.
take-all decline.why: Suppressive soil arising spontaneously - the field cures itself, given time and no fumigation.

TEP.text: Transparent exopolymer particles - sticky invisible gel produced by algae and bacteria, which aggregates into marine snow and, at scale, mucilage.
TEP.why: Stained with Alcian blue to be seen at all, which is why it went unnoticed until the 1990s.

terminal electron acceptor.text: The molecule an organism finally dumps electrons onto to extract energy from food. Oxygen is the best, and when it runs out life switches down a ladder - nitrate, manganese, iron, sulphate, then carbon dioxide.
terminal electron acceptor.why: Each step yields less energy, and each produces a different waste product. The sulphate step is why marine anoxia turns toxic.

thatch.text: A greasy organic mat that builds up in turf when material is produced faster than it decays. Caused by heavy fertilising, pesticides killing earthworms, and compaction.
thatch.why: The ordinary roofing word. Greenkeepers treat it by restoring the soil fauna, not by feeding the grass less.

thraustochytrid.text: Marine microbes in the same group as labyrinthulids, increasingly recognised as major decomposers of organic matter at sea - and farmed commercially for omega-3 oil.
thraustochytrid.why: Neither fungi nor algae nor animals, and absent from every category on a monitoring form.

toxicant.text: A poisonous substance, especially a manufactured one. Distinguished from a toxin, which strictly means a poison made by a living thing.
toxicant.why: The distinction matters in the literature and is routinely ignored elsewhere.

transduction.text: Genes moved between bacteria by a virus carrying them from one host to the next. A principal route of horizontal gene transfer, which makes viruses a cause of adaptation as well as of death.
transduction.why: One of three classical routes, alongside conjugation and taking up loose DNA from the water.

transect.text: A line along which measurements are taken at intervals - here, usually running from the shore into deeper water to find how deep plants still grow.

Trichoderma.text: A soil fungus sold commercially to protect crops, working partly by producing antifungal compounds and partly by occupying the space a pathogen would need.
Trichoderma.why: An ordinary agricultural product that is also a working demonstration of colonisation resistance.

trophic.text: To do with feeding - who eats whom, and at what level of the food web.
trophic.why: Greek trophe, nourishment. The same root as eutrophic and auxotroph.

trophic cascade.text: A change at one level of the food web propagating down through the levels beneath it - removing a predator releases its prey, which suppresses the level below.
trophic cascade.why: Greek trophe again, nourishment. Cascade because it falls through the levels.

turbid.text: Cloudy - water with enough suspended material in it to block light.
turbid.why: From Latin turba, a crowd or commotion: stirred-up. The same root gives turbine, a thing spun, and disturb. Cloudiness named after the stirring that causes it.

Type VI secretion system.text: A molecular spear one bacterium uses to inject toxins into a neighbour on contact. Bacteria do not only poison each other chemically; they stab.
Type VI secretion system.why: Contact-dependent, targeted, and aimed overwhelmingly at close relatives competing for the same space.

Vandkemi.text: Danish for water chemistry - the ODA category holding nutrient and contaminant concentrations from water samples.

vandområde.text: Danish for water body - the administrative unit Danish water policy is written in. There are 119 marine ones, and this project argues at length that the unit is not a natural one.

viral shunt.text: Viruses bursting bacteria and algae so that their carbon returns to dissolved organic matter instead of being eaten by something larger.
viral shunt.why: A shunt in the electrical sense: the current is diverted before it reaches the load.

virion.text: A single complete virus particle outside a cell. Marine water holds roughly ten million of them per millilitre.
virion.why: The unit you would count, as against the infection, which is what they do.

virioplankton.text: The viruses drifting in seawater - roughly ten million in every millilitre, and the most numerous biological entities in the ocean.
virioplankton.why: Virus plus plankton. Their existence at this scale was only established in 1989.

virome.text: All the viruses in or on an organism or in an environment. Most are uncharacterised, including the ones nearly every human carries permanently with no known effect.
virome.why: By count the largest part of any microbiome, and the least understood.

VMS.text: Vessel monitoring system - satellite position reports that fishing vessels are required to transmit, used to map where gear was actually worked.
VMS.why: The record exists; the fine-resolution version is not public.

washwater.text: Water used to scrub pollutants out of ship exhaust, then discharged to sea. It is acidic and carries metals and hydrocarbons, and discharging it is legal.
washwater.why: Exhaust gas cleaning moves the pollution from the air to the water; whether that is an improvement depends on which you were measuring.

Winkler.text: The chemical titration for dissolved oxygen, in use since 1888 and still the reference method against which sensors are checked.
Winkler.why: Lajos Winkler, who published it as a doctoral student.

Wolbachia.text: A bacterium introduced into mosquito populations to block dengue transmission. Released across whole cities and among the most successful vector-control interventions of the past decade.
Wolbachia.why: The flagship case of replacing a pesticide with an occupant rather than a poison.

zooplankton.text: The drifting animals - copepods, larvae, jellyfish - that eat phytoplankton and are eaten by fish.
